source: Kim (2026) When LLMs Sit Above Diagnostic Tools: Table 3 sensitivity analyses (TEP)
finding: An explicit arbitration instruction did not fix the TEP integration deficit. It cut harmful acceptances but raised missed corrections. Giving the stored unaided diagnosis made it worse. A random-forest specialist gave the same gap.
numbers: Specialist 83.3%. Primary implicit: integrated 77.4%, -5.9 [-12.0,-0.7], missed corrections 140/295 (47.5%), harmful 15/99 (15.2%). Explicit arbitration: 76.1%, -7.2 [-14.0,-1.3], missed 161/295 (54.6%), harmful 6/99 (6.1%); explicit minus implicit -1.3 [-3.1,+0.5]. Prior-label: 72.2%, -11.1 [-18.3,-3.6], missed 215/295 (72.9%), harmful 0/99. Random-forest specialist 84.0%, integrated 78.2%, -5.7 [-11.2,-1.1].
quote: Explicit arbitration did not improve integrated accuracy relative to the implicit condition
limits: Prompt-level arbitration only trades one error for the other. Sensitivity runs are not independent confirmations. Only one TEP set (150 runs, 6 classes), logistic or RF specialist. No trained selector tested.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on an 'arbitrate between sources' instruction to recover the better source. A trained or rule-based selector (a check outside the model) is the untested next step; the oracle ceiling is 92.76%.

source: Kim (2026) Sections 4.4-4.7 and Appendix B: bearing datasets, reasoning effort, Lam 9600
finding: Across bearing datasets implicit LLM integration rarely beat the stronger standalone source. Higher reasoning effort raised unaided accuracy but not integration. On real etch-tool data, wrong advice overturned correct LLM answers.
numbers: Of 22 eligible comparisons: 3 intervals below zero, 18 included zero, 1 above zero. All 28 CWRU point estimates below the stronger source. TEP high reasoning (4 models): unaided +5.2 [2.2,8.2]; integrated +2.2 [-0.2,4.8]; gap to better source -6.3 (low) vs -4.2 (high). Lam 9600: 6 of 23 initially correct judgments overturned by wrong advice across 4 wafers; paired repeats did not flip. CWRU 72 cases, Paderborn 87, XJTU-SY 88.
quote: Higher reasoning effort therefore should not be assumed to solve the integration problem
limits: Lam 9600 analysis is descriptive with controlled labels, not a benchmark. Specialist errors sparse on CWRU. Intervals not corrected for multiple comparisons.
agent_relevance: More thinking tokens help the LLM alone but do not remove the integration gap; check the tool, do not just think longer.

source: Kim (2026) Appendix M: NORMAL-class false alarms on TEP confirmation set
finding: On the 25 true-normal TEP runs the specialist raised many false alarms (56%), the unaided LLM few (4.6%), and the integrated output 9.7%. All 14 adopted false alarms copied the specialist's IDV15 label.
numbers: Specialist NORMAL-to-fault 14/25 = 56.0% [36.0,76.0]; unaided LLM 8/175 model-runs = 4.6% [0.6,9.7]; integrated 17/175 = 9.7% [5.7,14.3]. Integrated minus unaided +5.1 [-1.7,11.4]; minus specialist -46.3 [-63.4,-29.7]. Preserved NORMAL in 80 of 94 conflict cases (85.1%).
quote: This conditional classification error should not be interpreted as an operational plant alarm frequency
limits: Post hoc, 25 runs, closed 6-class labelling (not a streaming alarm rate). Not at fixed hit rate, so it only partly answers the false-alarm-cost gap.
agent_relevance: Closest measurement yet of LLM false-alarm cost: the LLM layer can suppress a noisy detector's false alarms, so resisting the tool is sometimes right.

source: Wei and Fink (2026) Agentic Root Cause Analysis through Evidence-Grounded Reasoning (AgentRCA), PRONTO real facility
finding: A zero-shot LLM agent that uses only normal-operation data plus fault text diagnosed faults on a real multiphase-flow rig at 87.6% top-1. Supervised models trained on faults did better with full data but worse with few labels.
numbers: PRONTO: test 105 windows (21 per class x 5 states), mean of 5 seeds. Random 20.0%. AgentRCA top-1 87.6%, top-2 96.8%. LightGBM 99.0%, AE+classifier 99.6%, MiniRocket+Ridge 94.5%. Best supervised baseline falls to 65.1% at small label counts; LightGBM needs at least 20 labelled fault windows per class to match top-1. Reasoning structure: unstructured 83.2/93.3, ReAct-like 85.4/95.6, hypothesis table 87.6/96.8 (top-1/top-2).
quote: only surpasses AgentRCA's Top-2 accuracy when trained on the full dataset
limits: PRONTO is a lab-scale real facility with 5 classes and a fixed fault vocabulary; this is diagnosis (which fault), not detection. Authors' own method; no independent replication.
agent_relevance: A positive real-data result for an LLM with a statistical tool and a hypothesis table. Support for keeping competing hypotheses explicit and for feeding the LLM computed evidence rather than raw numbers.

source: Wei and Fink (2026) AgentRCA, TEP extension and sample efficiency
finding: On the harder Tennessee Eastman process the same zero-shot agent got only 40.0% top-1 and 61.5% top-2. Supervised baselines with full labels got 78-86%, but need about 40 to 800 labelled windows per fault to beat the agent.
numbers: TEP 52 variables, 21 faults. AgentRCA 40.0% top-1, 61.5% top-2. Supervised full data: LightGBM 84.1%, AE+classifier 85.7%, MiniRocket+Ridge 78.5%. With 25 or fewer faulty windows per fault all supervised below 30%. LightGBM needs about 40 windows per fault to pass 40.0%; AE over 200; to match top-2 61.5%, 80 (LightGBM) to 800 (AE).
quote: This benchmark presents a significantly more challenging environment
limits: TEP windows and split not comparable with other TEP papers. Diagnosis of 21 faults, not detection.
agent_relevance: Confirms ambiguous TEP faults stay hard for LLM reasoning even with tools; sets a realistic ceiling.

source: Wei and Fink (2026) AgentRCA, computational cost
finding: One diagnostic window cost about five tool calls, 4,615 tokens and 51 seconds on a 30B open model. The authors say it is not meant to replace low-latency detectors.
numbers: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507: average 5 tool calls, 4,615 tokens, 51 s per window. Digital twin trained once on normal data.
quote: not intended to replace low-latency anomaly detectors for real-time alarm generation
limits: Token and time cost reported for AgentRCA only; no equal-token comparison against a statistical detector exists. Detection delay not measured.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete token price per diagnosis. Detection stays with the cheap statistical stage; the LLM acts after the flag.

source: Alhazmi (2026) Large reasoning models for abnormal situation management in safety-critical industrial processes
finding: A reasoning model above regulatory control, with a bounded checked action interface, kept a simulated plant in constraints in 39 of 39 abnormal scenarios and named the true fault in 15 of 15 safety-critical ones.
numbers: Plant-wide TEP-type benchmark (Bathelt kernel), 39 episodes (15 safety-gap), 3 noise seeds. Baseline in constraint 24/39 (0.615), 15 trips. Sonnet-5 high effort 39/39, diagnosis accuracy any invocation 0.846, US$2.32 per episode; low effort 38/39, 1 trip, diagnosis 0.769, US$1.31; GLM-5.2 37/39, US$0.67; DeepSeek-V4-Flash 39/39, US$0.07. Paired difference +0.385 [0.22,0.54], McNemar p = 6e-5. Reference controller also 39/39. Thirty-fold cost range, models not distinguishable (pairwise McNemar p over 0.5).
quote: It identifies the ground-truth tag on every safety-gap episode (15/15)
limits: Simulation only; closed 12-item diagnosis vocabulary given; the endpoint is reachable by a fixed rule table (authors say so); frozen suite of 39 scenarios. Not open detection.
agent_relevance: Diagnosis-then-act with checked actions works in simulation. Cheap models matched expensive ones, so spend effort on the verifier rather than the model.

source: Alhazmi (2026) matched-pair reasoning effort case and decision latency
finding: On the hardest scenario, low effort misdiagnosed a reactant-composition upset as valve stiction and the plant tripped. High effort diagnosed it right. Time to detect was not measured: decision latency was a fixed modelled 0.05 h.
numbers: Scenario S4: low effort tripped (stripper inventory hit high-level interlock at t = 11.6 h), high effort stabilised; one discordant pair of 39, McNemar p = 1.0 (no effect size claimed). Accepted action applied after modelled decision latency 0.05 h; provider latency logged separately. One scenario showed revision away from a correct initial diagnosis.
quote: provider latency does not enter simulated time and is logged separately
limits: Single case with an identified mechanism, not a statistical effect. Detection delay is not an outcome; onset of each injected disturbance is known.
agent_relevance: Confirms the delay gap is open for LLM agents. Also shows a failure mode to guard: revising away from a correct first diagnosis.

source: Zhou and Yu (2025) Can LLMs Understand Time Series Anomalies? (ICLR 2025)
finding: LLMs understand time series better as images than text, do not gain from explicit reasoning prompts, and can find trivial anomalies but there is no evidence for subtle real ones. A simple isolation-forest baseline still has higher plain F1 than the LLMs.
numbers: Controlled synthetic anomaly types; 21 prompt variants per model (13 text, 8 vision); GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-Flash and open models; metric affinity F1. Shortening series from 1000 to 300 steps improved text results consistently.
quote: we have no evidence that they can understand more subtle real-world anomalies
limits: Mainly synthetic series, zero- and few-shot, 2024 models. Baselines are Isolation Forest and thresholding, not an always-normal predictor. Not process plants.
agent_relevance: For raw numeric windows the LLM is weak; give it plots or computed summaries and keep series short. Supports sending numbers through a statistical tool first.

source: Wu and Keogh (2021) Current Time Series Anomaly Detection Benchmarks are Flawed
finding: Most exemplars of popular anomaly benchmarks are trivial, have unrealistic anomaly density, mislabelled truth or run-to-failure bias. A one-line detector solves most of them, so apparent progress may be illusory.
numbers: Yahoo benchmark: 316 of 367 series (86.1%) solved by a one-liner found by brute-force search over k, c, b. Four flaws: triviality, unrealistic anomaly density, mislabelled ground truth, run-to-failure bias.
quote: 316 out of 367 (86.1%) can be easily solved with a one-liner
limits: Tested on Yahoo, Numenta, NASA, OMNI; not on TEP and not on LLMs. Their remark that early-detection scoring is hard to interpret bears on delay metrics.
agent_relevance: Any LLM detection claim needs a trivial baseline (moving std, diff) on the same data. Our test harness should include one.

source: Constantinides et al. (2025) FailureSensorIQ (NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks)
finding: LLM knowledge of sensor-failure relationships is fragile: average 53.5% across frontier models, human experts 60.2% mean, large drops under perturbation.
numbers: 2,667 single-correct MCQs; models average 53.5%; human experts max 66.19%, mean 60.20% (3 participants). o1 60.4% original to 44.2% perturbed; llama-4-scout 54.0% to 24.1%; o3-mini ACC@Consist 47.5%.
quote: a significant drop in performance that is fragile to perturbations
limits: Multiple-choice question bank from ISO documents, not plant data. Tests knowledge, not detection.
agent_relevance: Control-loop and sensor knowledge in models is shaky; a retrieved sensor-failure table may help more than model memory. Not tested for faults 5, 10, 13.

source: Merzouki et al. (2026) FactoryBench: Evaluating Industrial Machine Understanding
finding: On real robot telemetry (cobot and arm faults), no frontier LLM exceeds 50% chance-corrected on the structured levels, and the ranking reshuffles on decision questions.
numbers: 69,691 Q&A items from about 15k episodes (UR3, KUKA, AURSAD, voraus-AD); six frontier LLMs zero-shot; four causal levels; L1-L3 leader is fourth of six on L4.
quote: no model exceeds 50% (chance-corrected) on the structured levels
limits: Robot telemetry, not process plants. Template-generated Q&A. Sim-to-real appendix not opened.
agent_relevance: Real industrial series are far from saturated for LLMs; test decision questions separately from state questions.

source: Gopaluni, Kotamraju and Bhushan (2026) LLMs in Process Systems Engineering (survey)
finding: Expert narrative survey: fault diagnosis with LLMs is at early or pilot stage, validated on simulation, with public benchmarks such as Tennessee Eastman and little real plant data.
numbers: Maturity table lists fault diagnosis as 'Early' with multi-agent and FD-LLM entries at 'Pilot'; validation level 'Simulation'; process control called the least mature use.
limits: Narrative survey, not systematic. No new numbers.
agent_relevance: Real-plant reproducibility of FaultExplainer or Chain of Physics gains is unestablished; treat as simulation evidence.

source: Wei and Fink (2026) AgentRCA ablations and report retrieval
finding: What mattered for the agent on PRONTO was the statistical evidence layer: operating-condition matching and signed z-scores. Technical-report retrieval raised top-1 accuracy.
numbers: Ablation top-1/top-2: full 87.6/96.8; no operating-condition matching 40.6/65.4; no signed z-scores 43.8/67.6; no autoencoder residuals 83.8/94.6. Late retrieval of technical reports gave the largest top-1 gain among retrieval variants (exact gain not recorded).
quote: Removing it drops Top-1 accuracy from 87.6% to 40.6%
limits: Single dataset, authors' ablations, mean of 5 seeds. Retrieval gain figure not captured.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge helps (a hint for control-loop knowledge on faults 5 and 10) but only after the numerical evidence is right.

source: Kim (2026) TEP confirmation set design (Appendix B)
finding: Kim's TEP protocol was frozen before evaluation and uses 150 runs over six classes. It is a small closed-set test, not a detection benchmark.
numbers: 150 simulation runs, 25 each from NORMAL, IDV1, IDV4, IDV6, IDV13, IDV15; development selection required enough specialist-LLM disagreement, so the 92.76% oracle gap describes a selected setting. Specialists: 400-tree random forest or multinomial logistic.
quote: the oracle gap describes this selected setting rather than what should be expected from an arbitrary specialist
limits: Faults 3 and 9 absent, faults 5 and 10 absent. Oracle gap may be inflated by selection.
agent_relevance: Protocol evidence for gap 3: LLM-on-TEP papers each use different subsets (Kim 6 classes; AgentRCA 21 faults; Alhazmi closed-loop kernel), so no common protocol exists yet.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Exploring LLM-based agentic frameworks for fault diagnosis, as described by Kim (2026)
finding: Only seen as a description in Kim 2026: Lee compared raw sensor windows with descriptive statistics and single- versus multi-model agent architectures.
limits: Not opened; description is second-hand. Earlier evidence c16 holds the numbers.
agent_relevance: Drift over repeated fault cycles (gap 8) is not resolved by anything opened here.

source: Kim (2026) related work on arbitration and ensembles (Kim 2026a, MemToC, TrustMargin) as described
finding: Related work cited by Kim shows the same pattern outside industry: oracle gains across model subsets are large but realised voting gains are small, and reference-free judges often fail to choose a better candidate.
numbers: Qualitative only; no figures read from the cited papers. Learning-to-defer methods train a routing objective; Kim tests only an off-the-shelf LLM.
quote: The improvement possible case by case can be much larger than the improvement actually delivered
limits: Second-hand description; cited papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports using a trained or rule-based selector, not LLM judgement alone, when merging detector and LLM.
